title: Chinese developer makes ARTEX AI agent closed-source after Korean bank hack
excerpt: Hong Kong Racing. World Racing. Analysis. Racecourse Entertainment. Lifestyle. Arts & Culture. Wellness. Food & Wine. Leisure. Showbiz. Entertainment. Gossip. Screen & Music. Sport. INNOVATION. 8 hours ago. AI Artificial Intelligence words are seen in this illustration taken, May 4, 2023. REUTERS. The Chinese developer of ARTEX said they have converted the AI agent to a closed-source project after cybersecurity firms identified it as a tool used in a recent cyberattack campaign against South Korean banks. "Given the misuse of the tool, the ARTEX project will no longer be updated and will be converted to closed source. No further versions will be released to the public nor will maintenance support be provided," the developer, who uses the GitHub handle "Autumn-27", said on the code-hosting platform on Thursday. They said the original aim of ARTEX was to help enterprises and organizations conduct security risk testing and improve their security capabilities. Without explicitly addressing the South Korean bank attacks, they said they opposed any illegal use of the software and bore no responsibility for conduct that violates laws and regulations. ARTEX's Github page has been taken down, according to Reuters' checks. US cybersecurity firm Crowdstrike said on Wednesday the suspect behind recent cyberattacks at South Korean banks aimed at stealing customers' personal data was likely a ​China-based 26-year-old who used the ARTEX AI agent and Anthropic's Claude Code. Released on GitHub this year, ARTEX is an open-source AI agent designed to automate penetration testing. It is not a standalone large language model but ⁠connects to ​external LLMs such as ChatGPT, Claude and DeepSeek to help organisations test for vulnerabilities in their ​networks. At least nine South Korean banks have disclosed or been reported by local media as targets of cyberattacks since late September, prompting police to launch ​a probe this week and President Lee Jae Myung to call for robust response measures. Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told a regular press briefing on Thursday that the ministry was not familiar with the ​case, adding that China consistently opposes and combats hacking activities. title: UBS only European bank in top 10 of AI adoption as JPMorgan Chase leads
excerpt: . UBS only European bank in top 10 of AI adoption as JPMorgan Chase leads. UBS is now the only European lender among the top 10 banks judged most advanced in adopting artificial intelligence, after HSBC dropped out of the top tier of the Evident AI Index, while JPMorgan Chase widened its lead and North American banks tightened their grip. Quirino Mealha. Wed 7 October 2026 at 12:45 am GMT-5 3 min read. UBSG. SW. Switzerland's UBS stands alone for Europe in the top ten of an annual league table measuring how far major banks have gone in putting AI to work, as North American lenders led by JPMorgan Chase pull further ahead. The ranking, published on Tuesday by Evident, a firm that tracks AI adoption in financial services, rates 50 large lenders in North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific using only public data. Banks are deploying the technology to catch fraud, write software, vet loans and help advisers serve clients, and the 50 lenders have made public over 1,100 distinct uses of AI since 2021. They are scored on AI talent, which carries the most weight, as well as innovation such as research and patents, leadership focus and transparency on responsible use. UBS climbed one place to sixth this year, while London-headquartered HSBC, eighth in 2025, slipped to 11th. European banks dominate the next ten places, including British lenders Lloyds Banking Group, unchanged in 15th, NatWest in 17th and Barclays, which rose four places to 19th. JPMorgan Chase, which ranked in the top two in all four categories, widened its lead over second-placed US lender Capital One. Royal Bank of Canada was third and Australia's CommBank fourth, with six US and two Canadian banks in the top ten. Evident found that the banks' AI capabilities improved almost three times as fast over the past year as in the three preceding years on average, the quickest progress since it began measuring in 2023. "This was the year AI in banking went industrial," said Alexandra Mousavizadeh, Evident's co-founder and co-CEO. Hiring, not firing. Evident also challenged the idea that AI will gut bank workforces, finding that the leaders are still recruiting AI specialists and prioritising growth over job cuts. That contrasts with London-based Standard Chartered, which said in May it would cut around 7,800 back-office jobs by 2030 as it leans on AI and automation. Software implementation roles grew 4. 3% across the 50 banks over the past year. US bank Morgan Stanley is reinvesting more than one million developer hours freed up by its DevGen. AI platform rather than trimming IT teams, while UBS's STAAT Insights tool saves its advisers roughly 1,200 hours a week. "Roles are changing, and some are not being backfilled, but the banks at the top of our Index are growing, and growing headcount," Mousavizadeh stated. Twelve banks now report a realised or projected return on AI, up from eight, including newcomer Lloyds, which said in January that generative AI delivered around £50 million (€58. 8mn) in value in 2025 and should add more than £100 million (€117. 6mn) this year. "With AI budgets at record levels, the banks that can prove their returns will keep the money flowing to the right places," said Daniel Shackleford Capel, managing director of banking at Evident. Amid growing concern over keeping ever more capable AI under control, 80% of the leading banks have advanced safeguards, such as checks on the data that models use and the answers they give, against 40% of the remaining banks in the index. In the EU, AI used to assess people's creditworthiness is classed as high-risk under the AI Act, though the rules for such systems were pushed back in July to December 2027. Evident plans to add a fifth pillar to the index in 2027, measuring the outcomes banks actually achieve from AI. Terms and Privacy Policy. Privacy dashboard.

title: Hackers used AI to steal 70,000 bank data records; South Korea launches large-scale investigation.
excerpt: . Hackers used AI to steal 70,000 bank data records; South Korea launches large-scale investigation. (CLO) A number of major banks in South Korea have been victims of a large-scale cyberattack involving artificial intelligence (AI), resulting in the leakage of approximately 70,000 customer records. President Lee Jae Myung has ordered a full-scale response, and South Korean police officially launched an urgent investigation on October 6th. Công Luận • 06/10/2026. Speaking at a ministerial council meeting, President Lee Jae Myung emphasized: "In some cyberattack incidents, there have been indications that AI has been used, causing considerable concern and unease among the public. ". In response to this situation, the South Korean leader requested "clarification of the situation, while focusing manpower and resources to minimize damage as much as possible. " On October 6th, South Korean police officially launched a large-scale investigation into the cyberattack that leaked the personal information of numerous customers. Previously, on October 2nd, the Korean Financial Services Commission (FSC) first confirmed that a series of major banks had been attacked. On October 4th, FSC Chairman Lee Eog-weon convened an emergency meeting with representatives from financial associations, regulatory agencies, and leaders of affected organizations. He stated, "We cannot rule out the possibility that the attacks used AI. ". You may also like. This widespread cyberattack severely impacted seven financial institutions, leaking approximately 68,000 to 70,000 personal customer data records in South Korea. The first incident was discovered on September 30th at Shinhan Bank, where loan application data for approximately 25,000 to 25,729 customers was leaked, including their names, phone numbers, annual income, and credit limits. Subsequently, KB Kookmin Bank and Hana Bank recorded 119 and 89 affected cases, respectively. Woori Bank and NH NongHyup Bank also detected unusual access but successfully blocked it in time. Yegaram Savings Bank suffered the largest data leak affecting approximately 40,000 customers starting on September 30th. Additionally, an internal audit on October 3rd at Welcome Savings Bank confirmed that data from around 2,200 corporate customers had been leaked. Traces on the server indicate that the attacker used an AI-based penetration testing tool called "Artex AI" to automatically scan for vulnerabilities and select the next intrusion method. ". AI-powered financial attacks in South Korea reflect a growing global trend of cybersecurity threats. title: AI should not make final decisions in wealth management
excerpt: Artificial intelligence can transform wealth management, but firms must ensure humans retain responsibility for final decisions as AI moves closer to client-facing activities, according to Eric Moy, chief executive of KBQuest and an adjunct assistant professor at HKU Business School. Speaking at a luncheon on AI-powered wealth management in Hong Kong, Moy warned against allowing AI to manage an entire workflow independently. “No company should allow AI to make the final decision,” he said. Hong Kong regulations require a human to provide final approval. Liability therefore remains with the individual adviser, the institution and its senior leadership rather than with the technology itself. Instead, he recommended combining AI with rule-based software and human review in a “human-in-the-loop” process. By alternating AI-generated outputs with verification and oversight, organizations can improve reliability while reducing operational risk, he said. Moy (pictured) argued that most firms deploying AI are starting in back-office functions – operations and compliance – because the risks are lower and efficiency gains are easier to demonstrate compared to front-line advisory functions. Account opening, compliance checks and operational workflows offer immediate opportunities to automate repetitive tasks while improving speed and accuracy, he said. Moy drew a distinction between using AI directly to perform a task and using AI to build deterministic, rule-based systems that then execute workflows. The latter approach, he argued, provides greater accuracy and control because decisions are governed by predefined rules rather than left entirely to a model’s judgment. In the front office, Moy said AI could help relationship managers search products, construct portfolio proposals, explain complex investment materials and simulate alternative scenarios in real time. Rather than waiting days or weeks to revise recommendations after receiving client feedback, advisers could use interactive AI-powered tools to adjust portfolios instantly and illustrate the implications to clients. Yet the closer AI moves toward investment advice, the greater the risks become. Moy highlighted potential problems including unsuitable recommendations, regulatory breaches, mis-selling, inaccurate risk representation and legal exposure. The biggest danger, however, is a relationship manager telling a client that a recommendation came from the AI system. Beyond advisory functions, Moy sees AI playing an important role in governance and compliance. Traditional monitoring often occurs after a transaction has been completed, but AI could enable compliance reviews in real time or near real time, identifying unusual activity or data anomalies as transactions occur. A critical prerequisite for broader adoption, he said, is the creation of a corporate “memory layer” hosted within an organization’s own environment. Sending sensitive corporate information to externally hosted AI models raises confidentiality concerns, while building internal data infrastructure and cybersecurity protections requires significant investment. Nevertheless, Moy described such a data layer as essential for meaningful enterprise AI deployment. He also identified organizational alignment, poor data readiness and the cost of running models and internal data structures as major barriers to adoption. Firms should classify initiatives according to low, medium and high risk and prioritize lower-risk projects first, he said. Moy outlined what he called an AI risk ladder. Lower-risk applications include document summarization, policy searches and information retrieval. Medium-risk uses include portfolio scenario generation, product monitoring and client-meeting preparation. High-risk applications involve investment recommendations, client-facing research, trade execution and decisions that could affect customer outcomes or money movement. title: HSBC to Cut Up to 70% of UK Wealth Advisers as It Adopts Artificial Intelligence
excerpt: HSBC to Cut Up to 70% of UK Wealth Advisers as It Adopts Artificial Intelligence. By. Distilled Post Editorial Team. HSBC intends to make substantial reductions to the workforce in its UK wealth management division, as the bank integrates artificial intelligence into its daily operations. The plan, set out in a report on the restructuring, affects management, specialist and advisory staff. Approximately half of the management and specialist positions in the division are due to be eliminated. Among financial advisers, reductions could reach 70 per cent. A formal consultation period is under way, and staff who are leaving are expected to depart by the end of October. The bank has not disclosed the total headcount of the unit. The division currently employs hundreds of relationship managers across the country, which gives some indication of the numbers involved. HSBC responded to questions about the restructuring with a short statement. "HSBC UK is a long-established, leading UK wealth manager and premium banking provider," it said. The bank added that it is continuing to evolve to deliver more digitally enabled products and journeys to support its wealth service and meet the changing needs of customers. It did not comment on the number of roles affected or on the role of AI in the decision. The restructuring follows the direction set by Georges Elhedery, who became chief executive in 2024. Speaking at an investor event in May, Elhedery said employees would need to adapt to technological change. He stated directly that generative AI would lead to job losses. The cuts in the wealth division are the first large-scale application of that position to a customer-facing UK business, based on the information available. Wealth management has traditionally depended on personal relationships between advisers and clients, particularly those with substantial assets. Relationship managers handle portfolio reviews, retirement planning and the sale of investment products. Many of these tasks involve routine analysis and documentation, which software can now produce faster and at lower cost. Banks have therefore identified advisory services as an area where automation can reduce expenditure without removing the client-facing function entirely. HSBC is not alone in pursuing this approach. Major banking institutions are increasing capital investment in AI tools. These systems are being used to simplify administrative processes, draft and personalise client communications, and lower operating costs. Several lenders have said publicly that headcount in back-office and support functions is likely to fall as the technology matures. The scale of the planned reduction at HSBC, with up to seven in ten advisers affected, is larger than most of those earlier disclosures. The consequences extend beyond the bank. Financial services is one of the largest employers of white-collar workers in the United Kingdom, and economists are monitoring how quickly automation will alter demand for skilled roles in the sector. Advisers hold professional qualifications and regulatory permissions that take years to acquire. Workers displaced from a single large employer may find a limited number of equivalent vacancies if competitors adopt similar plans at the same time. Questions also remain about service quality and regulation. Advice on investments and pensions is subject to strict rules on suitability, and firms must be able to show that customers receive guidance appropriate to their circumstances. A reduction of this size will draw attention to how HSBC intends to maintain compliance while serving clients with fewer human advisers. The bank has not set out those arrangements in its statement. The outcome of the consultation will determine the final number of redundancies. Until it concludes, the precise effect on the workforce and on customers will remain uncertain. title: AI-powered automated payments exceeding 10 million VND per transaction are classified as high-risk.
excerpt: . AI-powered automated payments exceeding 10 million VND per transaction are classified as high-risk. The State Bank of Vietnam has recently issued Circular 53/2026 regulating safety, risk management, and deployment conditions for the application of artificial intelligence systems in the banking sector. For AI systems that automatically perform electronic transactions in banking operations, a system is identified as high-risk if it performs at least one of the following types of transactions. Báo Thanh niên • 08/10/2026. The circular was issued to specify the regulations of the Artificial Intelligence Law and related guiding documents, and to establish a unified framework for safety, risk management, and conditions for deploying AI systems in the banking industry. In recent times, banking units have accelerated the application of AI in many operations such as credit scoring, loan appraisal, payment fraud detection, automated consulting, eKYC, etc. Besides the benefits, the application of AI also gives rise to new risks related to cybersecurity, data security, model risk, third-party and supply chain risks, thereby impacting the legitimate rights and interests of organizations and individuals, and the safety of banking operations. PHOTO: NGOC THANG. You may also like. The Circular is developed using a risk-based management approach, ensuring that management requirements are commensurate with the level of risk and the scope of impact of each AI system, while also guaranteeing mechanisms for human supervision and intervention. The main contents of the Circular specifically include classifying AI systems according to risk levels and ensuring mechanisms for human supervision and intervention. This includes classifying AI systems, determining risk levels, and establishing appropriate mechanisms for human supervision and intervention; ensuring that AI does not replace human responsibilities and authority in banking operations. The regulations specify high-risk AI systems in the banking sector according to Decision No. 33/2026 of the Prime Minister, which promulgates the List of High-Risk Artificial Intelligence Systems. For AI systems that automatically execute payment transactions, a system is identified as high-risk when it automatically executes transactions with a value exceeding VND 10 million per transaction or a total daily value exceeding VND 20 million for individual customers; or over VND 50 million per transaction or a total daily value exceeding VND 100 million for institutional customers. For AI systems that automatically decide on credit granting, a system is identified as high-risk when it processes credit applications of VND 50 million or more. Enhance cybersecurity and data security. AI systems must undergo cybersecurity testing and assessment before official operation and periodically or whenever significant changes occur; simultaneously, meet requirements for data security, change management, incident handling, logging, and control of AI-specific risks. Establishing a risk management framework for AI system applications: The circular stipulates responsibilities for risk management, impact assessment for high-risk AI systems, and risk management based on three lines of defense; it also manages risks related to models, ethics, outsourcing, and supply chains. You may also like. Regarding the conditions for deploying AI systems, before officially putting the AI ​​system into operation, units must prepare dossiers as prescribed, conduct an assessment of the deployment conditions, and submit them to the competent authority for consideration and decision on officially putting the system into operation. title: UAE Business: Emirates NBD launches UAE’s first bank-led AI travel assistant
excerpt: Emirates NBD has launched the UAE’s first bank-led AI Travel Assistant, developed in collaboration with Visa and Tripadvisor, as the bank expands its digital offering beyond traditional financial services. The conversational platform is designed to help users research, plan and experience travel through personalised recommendations, itineraries and travel offers. The launch responds to growing demand for digital and AI-enabled travel planning among UAE residents, with the average traveller planning seven trips annually. Research also indicates that 50% of consumers across EMEA are comfortable booking holiday accommodation through AI platforms. Rohit Garg, Group Head of Retail Products and Chief Digital Officer of Retail Banking and Wealth Management at Emirates NBD, said: “The launch of our AI Travel Assistant marks another significant milestone in establishing Emirates NBD as a pioneer in AI-driven, customer-centric digital solutions. Travel is a major lifestyle driver for residents across the UAE. By combining cutting-edge AI with world-class insights from our partners, we are empowering travellers with innovative and personalised digital experiences that simplifies the process for our customers around one of their biggest passion points, namely travel, while unlocking exceptional value. ”. The assistant allows users to describe their preferences, budget and travel style through a conversational interface before receiving tailored itineraries, destination recommendations and lesser-known attractions. The platform draws on Tripadvisor’s database of more than 1 billion reviews and 8 million listings, with enhanced customisation available across the 15 destinations most favoured by UAE travellers. The collaboration combines Emirates NBD’s digital capabilities with Tripadvisor’s travel data and Visa’s payments expertise. The assistant can also identify relevant Visa cardholder benefits, including hotel discounts and car rental offers, helping users manage travel spending. Salima Gutieva, Visa’s VP and Country Manager for UAE, said: "Travelers today expect experiences that are personalised, intuitive and seamlessly integrated into their digital lives. By collaborating with Emirates NBD and Tripadvisor, we are making it easier for Visa cardholders to discover destinations, plan their journeys and access valuable travel benefits along the way. This initiative demonstrates how innovation, trusted partnerships and AI can come together to create smarter, more seamless and rewarding travel experiences. ". The AI Travel Assistant is available in English and is free to use through the Emirates NBD website and a dedicated Tripadvisor domain. Users do not need to be Emirates NBD customers or log in to a bank account to access the service. The launch forms part of Emirates NBD’s broader strategy to develop ecosystem-led digital banking and lifestyle solutions, positioning the bank as a provider of connected experiences extending beyond conventional financial services. -TradeArabia News Service.

Available through Bison Mobile, the Bison Bank's digital app, the tool brings together information on portfolios, markets and trends, while also strengthening access to the Bank's Financial Advisers, who support clients in the management of their wealth and in decisions related to their assets. With this new feature, clients' experience shall be significantly improved, as they will have a clearer and more dynamic view of their investment portfolio, enabling them to stratify it in different dimensions and to monitor its performance and market behaviour in a more integrated way. Supported by AI and developed in partnership with Nextvestment – a Singapore-based platform created for worldwide regulated wealth managers – the solution and its chatbot help answer questions about investments, interpret real-time data and identify opportunities, risks and trends in a way that is tailored to each client's profile. In addition to this more immediate reading of portfolios and markets, the new experience makes it possible to explore scenarios, compare asset classes or markets, and obtain suggested analyses aligned with the investment profile, time horizon and risk tolerance. This information also supports the preparation of more relevant conversations with Financial Advisers: through Bison Insight, clients can schedule a meeting directly in their Financial Adviser's calendar, having the Adviser received, in advance, the context of the client's searches and questions, enabling them to enhance the meeting preparation process, with more relevant information. Although it is based on an innovative technological component, Bison Insight does not replace specialised advice or the client's decision-making. On the contrary, it adds a layer of information and analysis that supports the Bank's Investment Advisory experience and helps bring digital innovation closer to wealth management. "Bison Insight reflects how we want to evolve the Private Banking experience, combining technology with personalised support. In a context in which clients have access to increasing amounts of information, it is essential to provide tools that help them interpret it, compare it and turn it into useful knowledge for more informed decisions. It is precisely this balance between digital innovation and human proximity that we seek to strengthen with this solution," says António Henriques, CEO of Bison Bank. The service will be launched in phases, with an initial controlled validation stage, followed by broader availability to clients eligible for the Investment Advisory service. This approach will allow the Bank to monitor the user experience, gather feedback and continue developing new features. The tool is already available in English and will gradually be adapted into Portuguese and Mandarin. About Bison Bank: Bison Bank, S. According to Mukomberanwa, major changes in the banking sector in 2018-’19 led to a shift in thinking that put digital solutions at the forefront of the business. However, the bank saw the potential for problems that might arise from relying on AI and recognised the need to create guidelines for its use. “We saw it fitting to partner with a reputable academic institution, combining our financial and industry expertise with the university’s strength in data science, computational thinking, and ethics to find a solution that shapes practical approaches to responsible AI adoption in the business landscape,” said Mukomberanwa. title: AI-powered automated banking transactions: How do new regulations protect customers?
excerpt: . AI-powered automated banking transactions: How do new regulations protect customers?. (GLO) - The State Bank of Vietnam has strict regulations on the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in the banking sector. Notably, customers have the right to temporarily suspend or cancel automated transactions and request a review of AI-generated decisions when they have complaints. Báo Gia Lai • 09/10/2026. The State Bank of Vietnam has recently issued Circular No. 53/2026/TT-NHNN regulating safety, risk management, and conditions for deploying artificial intelligence (AI) systems in the banking sector. The Circular sets out numerous requirements to protect customer rights, control automated decisions, and determine the responsibilities of service providers. This circular applies to credit institutions, branches of foreign banks, payment intermediary service providers, credit information companies, mobile money service providers, and a number of other entities in the banking sector. According to regulations, before deployment, AI systems must be classified according to risk level: high, medium, or low. An AI system that automatically processes payment transactions is classified as high risk if individual customer transactions exceed 10 million VND per transaction or the total daily transaction value exceeds 20 million VND. For institutional customers, the corresponding thresholds are over 50 million VND per transaction or over 100 million VND per day. You may also like. AI-powered systems that automatically recommend credit approvals also fall into the high-risk category if the credit amount is 50 million VND or more. For automated payment transactions, the bank and the customer must have a prior agreement specifying the scope of the transaction, limits, validity period, and the right to terminate the agreement. The total daily transaction value must not exceed the internal limit and must not exceed VND 100 million for individual clients and VND 500 million for institutional clients. Clients must be provided with tools to proactively pause or cancel automatic trading privileges. The circular also requires customers to be notified when they are interacting with AI and the system replaces humans in face-to-face communication. When a customer complains about an automated decision, that decision must be reviewed by a human; the review results will be the final basis for resolution. For decisions that directly affect a customer's financial obligations, legal liability, or access to services, the provider must retain records of the basis and key elements leading to the decision for explanation upon request. You may also like. Notably, outsourcing AI services does not alter the bank's responsibility for operational safety and customer rights. Third parties are prohibited from using the bank's data to train, refine, or improve the model without written consent. Circular No. 53/2026/TT-NHNN takes effect from November 15th. title: Nigeria emerging as one of Africa’s AI hubs —World Bank
excerpt: Business Nigeria emerging as one of Africa’s AI hubs —World Bank. Published by Tribune Online. October 9, 2026 6:30 am. NIGERIA is emerging as one of Africa’s leading centres of Artificial Intelligence activity, alongside Kenya and South Africa, according to the World Bank. According to News Agency of Nigeria (NAN), the Bank said AI activity on the continent was currently concentrated in the three economies, although adoption remained at an early stage across most African countries. The finding is contained in the World Bank’s latest Africa Economic Update, which places special focus on “Building AI-Readiness” across Sub-Saharan Africa. The report identifies Artificial Intelligence as a potentially powerful tool for raising productivity, creating jobs and improving delivery of essential services across the continent. According to the bank, Africa does not necessarily need to compete with advanced economies in developing the world’s most sophisticated frontier AI systems. Instead, it said the continent’s greatest immediate opportunity lies in adopting affordable, locally adapted AI applications capable of solving everyday development problems. Such applications could be deployed in education, agriculture, healthcare, finance, logistics and public administration. The bank said low-bandwidth AI tools could, for instance, support student learning and help farmers identify and manage livestock diseases. They could also help small businesses automate routine functions such as accounting and improve productivity. Andrew Dabalen, World Bank Chief Economist for the Africa Region, said African governments should build the foundations required to take advantage of the technology. He said investment in an AI-ready economy could unlock productivity gains, spur innovation and accelerate structural transformation. “The next challenge is turning growth into more jobs and better opportunities,” Dabalen said. “By investing in the foundations of an AI-ready economy, African countries can unlock productivity gains, spur innovation, and accelerate the structural transformation needed to raise living standards and reduce poverty. ”. READ ALSO: FG trains 200,000 Nigerians in artificial intelligence. The Bank, however, warned that significant infrastructure and institutional gaps could prevent many African countries from fully benefiting from the emerging technology. It identified reliable electricity, affordable internet connectivity, digital skills, quality data and computing infrastructure among the critical requirements for successful AI adoption. Effective governance, strong institutions and technical capacity would also be necessary to ensure that AI contributes to development rather than widening existing inequalities. The Bank called for greater regional cooperation, including through the African Union’s Continental AI Strategy and the African Continental Free Trade Area. It said such cooperation could help African countries scale AI-enabled solutions and generate more and better jobs. Separate World Bank research involving 4,205 firms across seven economies, including Nigeria, also found rapid growth in business adoption of AI. The research found that AI adoption rates among firms surveyed nearly tripled between 2024 and 2025, although sophisticated uses of the technology remained highly concentrated. It said managers in developing economies expected AI adoption to have positive effects on productivity and employment over the next three years. In dieser Rubrik nehmen Autorinnen und Autoren Stellung zu Wirtschafts- und Finanzthemen. Künstliche Intelligenz verändert unser Geschäft in einem Tempo, das noch vor wenigen Jahren kaum vorstellbar gewesen wäre. Was zunächst als einfache technologische Entwicklung erschien, ist heute zu einer strukturellen Transformation geworden. KI optimiert Portfolios, vervielfacht die Analysefähigkeiten und automatisiert zahlreiche standardisierte Prozesse. Diese Entwicklung ist Realität. Wer sie ignoriert, begeht einen strategischen Fehler. «Weil digitale Werkzeuge zum Standard werden, verlieren sie ihren Charakter als Unterscheidungsmerkmal. ». Gleichzeitig wird Technologie zunehmend zur Selbstverständlichkeit. Kunden erwarten heute, dass moderne digitale Werkzeuge in Finanzdienstleistungen integriert werden. Sie schaffen Effizienz, Präzision und Skalierbarkeit. Doch gerade, weil sie zum Standard werden, verlieren sie ihren Charakter als entscheidendes Unterscheidungsmerkmal. Die Zukunft der Vermögensberatung entscheidet sich deshalb nicht an der Frage, ob Technologie eingesetzt wird, sondern daran, wie sie mit menschlicher Expertise kombiniert wird. Vertrauen als nachhaltiger Wettbewerbsvorteil. Oft wird angenommen, dass die Interaktion zwischen Kunden und Banken künftig überwiegend zwischen Mensch und Maschine stattfinden wird. Diese Sichtweise unterschätzt eine grundlegende anthropologische Realität: Menschen brauchen Menschen. Persönliche Beziehungen sind kein Auslaufmodell, sondern ein elementarer Bestandteil unseres Zusammenlebens – und damit auch einer vertrauensvollen Beratung, die nur durch zwischenmenschliche Interaktion entstehen kann. Die Covid-Pandemie hat eindrücklich gezeigt, wie belastend der Verlust menschlicher Kontakte sein kann und wie gross umgekehrt die Freude war, als direkte Gespräche und persönliche Treffen wieder möglich wurden. Digitalisierung hat in dieser Phase vieles ermöglicht, sie konnte den menschlichen Austausch jedoch nie ersetzen. Daraus lässt sich auch für die Beratung eine klare Erkenntnis ableiten: Persönliche Beziehungen bleiben strukturell unverzichtbar. Diese Realität bestätigt sich täglich in Gesprächen mit wohlhabenden Familien. Hinter jedem Vermögen stehen individuelle Lebensgeschichten, Ziele, Bedürfnisse und Prioritäten. Keine Situation gleicht der anderen. Anlageentscheidungen hängen nicht allein von Renditeerwartungen ab, sondern von Lebenszielen, der Risikobereitschaft, dem Anlagehorizont, rechtlichen und steuerlichen Rahmenbedingungen oder internationalen Strukturen. Hinzu kommen familiäre Fragestellungen, insbesondere wenn mehrere Generationen eingebunden sind und teilweise unterschiedliche Interessen miteinander in Einklang gebracht werden müssen. «Gute Beratung entsteht nicht nur aus Daten, sondern aus dem Verständnis für die Person, die hinter den Daten steht. ». Gerade im Segment vermögender Kunden nimmt diese Komplexität weiter zu.
